claims.text: Limited free atomic mobility during reduction governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
With five or more atom types and limited mobility, stochastic incorporation makes random alloy formation more likely.
Sharply constrained mobility produces a homogeneous, single-phase alloy.
Greater atomic diffusion causes phase separation or elemental segregation.
A solid or quasi-solid single-source precursor containing five or more noble metal salts is an appropriate initial state for the proposed mechanism.
Rapid heating followed by immediate quenching at moderate temperature sharply restricts atomic mobility.
Slower cooling or extended reaction time permits greater atomic mobility than immediate quenching.
Limited diffusion kinetically traps a stochastic elemental arrangement in the forming nanoparticles.
Restricted mobility makes individual reduction events spatially isolated.
For five-element mixtures with limited mobility, stochastic incorporation can overcome differences in reduction sequence and preferences arising from element interactions or mixing enthalpies.
Five-element mixtures form a single phase more readily than binary mixtures under the reported single-source precursor reaction conditions.
The rapid, mobility-limited process will produce nanoparticles with a uniform single-phase alloy.
The rapid, mobility-limited process will produce a high degree of surface-exposed active sites.
The higher-mobility condition will produce phase separation, elemental segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed mechanism should extend to noble metal systems using similar solid, mixed single-source precursors at moderate temperatures.
The mechanism may not apply to high-temperature or solution-phase synthesis because atomic mobility is inherently high and additional kinetic factors dominate.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as the less-restricted, higher-mobility condition, but the predicted outcome describes the higher-mobility condition as showing segregation 'relative to the baseline.' This makes the comparison arm and baseline effectively the same condition rather than distinct comparators.
